The light key ingests group spellings on

Source: R/md-light-key.R
md_light_key.Rd

When an ingest collapses a source's rows to one name per EIN, it groups them on this key and keeps the most frequent raw spelling in each group (md_modal_sql()). The key is deliberately light: it merges spellings that differ only in how they are typed, and leaves everything else - misspellings, abbreviations, word order - for the normalizer's derived columns. So FOUNDATION and FOUNDAITON stay apart here.

Usage

md_light_key(x)

Arguments

x

A character vector.

Value

A character vector of keys; NA becomes "".

Details

The rule is npmatch's own name cleaning (.np_basic_clean()), so a key built here and a key npmatch builds for a query agree. The steps, in order:

  1. Accent marks are removed: É to E, ñ to n, ö to o.

  2. Letters that are not an accented form of another letter are written the way English text writes them: Ø to O, Ł to L, Đ to D, ı to i, Æ to AE, Œ to OE, ß and ẞ to SS, Þ to TH (npmatch's .np_special_letters).

  3. & becomes the word AND, so "A & B", "A&B" and "A AND B" are one.

  4. Uppercase.

  5. Joiners are deleted: every apostrophe (' ‘ ’ ʼ ´ `) and any period between two letters or digits. "BO'S PLACE" is "BOS PLACE" and "F.I.N.D." is "FIND", as the BMF holds them. A period that already separates words keeps its break: "ST. LUKES" is "ST LUKES".

  6. Every other character outside A-Z and 0-9 becomes a space: punctuation, tabs and newlines, and any non-Latin character. So "WINSTON-SALEM", "A/B" and "SMITH,JONES" keep two words each.

  7. Runs of spaces become one; leading and trailing spaces go.

History. Until 2026-10-25 (morning) steps 1-3 did not exist and every non-alphanumeric character was deleted: "CAFÉ" became "CAF", & vanished while AND was kept, and a tab joined two words. The first fix kept deletion for punctuation, which glued "WINSTON-SALEM" into one word where npmatch keeps two; steps 5-6 now follow npmatch exactly.

One known residual: npmatch transliterates with ICU's Latin-ASCII, which also spells out rarer forms (ligatures such as "ﬁ", for example). SQL has no Latin-ASCII, so here those become a space. They are vanishingly rare in organisation names.

Ingests compute the key in SQL through the macro md_light_key(x) (installed by .md_light_key_macro()); this R function is the same rule, and a test holds the two to identical output.
